6.3.1. Rural Primary Health Care Services

Primary healthcare services for the residents of 12,518 Village Panchayats and 472 Town Panchayats in Tamil Nadu are delivered through an extensive network of Rural Primary Health Centres (PHCs). These centres are established in accordance with the norms prescribed by the Government of India, at the rate of one PHC for every 30,000 population in plain areas and one PHC for every 20,000 population in hilly and difficult-toaccess areas. While establishing PHCs, due consideration is given to accessibility, availability of healthcare services and maintaining a minimum distance of 8 kilometres from the nearest existing

321

health institution to ensure the equitable distribution of healthcare facilities.

The rural primary healthcare system is supported by a multidisciplinary team comprising Medical Officers, Staff Nurses, Pharmacists, Laboratory Technicians, Health Inspectors, Village Health Nurses and Multi purpose Hospital workers.

Of 1,832 PHCs functioning across the State, 1,820 operate in Government-owned buildings, 11 function in rent-free buildings and 1 function in a rented building.

A total of 424 PHCs have been upgraded as Upgraded Primary Health Centres (UGPHCs) with 30-bedded facilities to provide round-the-clock inpatient and emergency care, thereby strengthening access to rural healthcare and reducing the referral burden.

The Government of Tamil Nadu will further strengthen primary health care services in rural areas by expanding PHC coverage, enhancing infrastructure, augmenting human resources and leveraging digital health technologies.

322

6.3.2. Urban Primary Health Care Services

Tamil Nadu is one of the most urbanised States in India, with around 50 percent of its population residing in urban areas, including 25 Municipal Corporations and 150 Municipalities.

Urban primary healthcare services are provided under the National Urban Health Mission (NUHM) through 504 Urban Primary Health Centres (UPHCs & UCHCs), established as per the norm of one UPHC for every 50,000 population, with a special focus on vulnerable and underserved communities.

These centres provide 12 comprehensive primary healthcare services, namely maternal healthcare, child healthcare, adolescent healthcare, mental healthcare, management of communicable and non-communicable diseases, elderly care, palliative care, ophthalmic care, ENT services and oral healthcare services.

In addition, 39 Urban Community Health Centres (UCHCs), established for every 2.5 lakh population, along with 154 Urban Polyclinics, provide specialist outpatient services and strengthen referral care in urban areas.

The White Paper on fiscal management of Tamil Nadu that was published in June 2026 sets the roadmap for better revenue mobilisation and administrative reforms, and has inter alia observed that the decline across major taxes like GST, VAT, and excise including revenues from mines and minerals has been mainly driven by administrative choices, leakages and corruption in the past rather than an underlying economic slowdown. It has also indicated that resolving this shortfall requires long-term, multi-year reforms focused on curbing corruption, enforcing compliance, and mobilizing resources efficiently. Some of the key factors highlighted in the White Paper are outlined below:

e Own-tax effort at a historic low — the SOTR-to-GSDP ratio fell to 5.45% in 2025-26, the lowest in two decades showing the sharpest decline among peer States in recent years.

e Large revenue foregone — decline in SOTR amounts to about Rs.1.23 lakh crore of annual revenue foregone, roughly 90% of the fiscal deficit in 2025-26.

e Unique to Tamil Nadu — Peer States like Maharashtra, and Karnataka have held on or have shown growth in SoTR-GSDP ratio, while Tamil Nadu alone has registered a steady decline.

e Broad-based weakness — the fall is reflected in all major taxes: GST, VAT on petroleum, State Excise, Stamp Duty and Motor Vehicle Tax.

e Cause is administrative, not structural — attributed to leakages, systemic corruption and administrative choices, primarily in commercial taxes, registration, excise and mining.

CHAPTER - V

ELECTRONICS CORPORATION OF

TAMIL NADU LIMITED (ELCOT)

5.1 Introduction

Electronics Corporation of Tamil Nadu

Limited, incorporated on 21 March 1977, is

entering its 50th year as a driving force behind

Tamil Nadu’s digital transformation and

diversified IT sector growth across the State.

Established with a focus on electronics,

electromedical and space technologies related

businesses and manufacturing, ELCOT has

progressively transformed from an organization

focused on electronic manufacturing into a key

technology arm of the Government. Its mandate

expanded to IT procurement and e-Governance

in 1999, followed by the development of IT

Parks, IT Towers and State Data Centre

infrastructure after 2005. Today, it plays a

117

strategic role in IT infrastructure development,

IT policy implementation and Government

technology procurement in supporting

Tamil Nadu’s digital transformation.

A key pillar of ELCOT’s mission is

promoting balanced regional growth through the

decentralization of the IT industry. As a strategic

anchor investor, ELCOT has developed world-

class IT parks and towers across Tier-II and

Tier-III cities, ensuring that the benefits of the

digital economy extend across the State.

ELCOT also serves as a key procurement

arm of the Government of

Tamil Nadu for IT hardware and services. This

unique dual role—as both a catalyst for frontier

technologies and a trusted provider of critical

digital governance services—reinforces ELCOT’s

pivotal place in Tamil Nadu’s development

journey.

118

Building on this legacy, ELCOT is

accelerating its strategic focus on frontier

technologies such as Artificial Intelligence (AI),

Quantum Computing, and AVGC-XR (Animation,

Visual Effects, Gaming, Comics, and Extended

Reality). Strengthening this vision, ELCOT is

establishing specialized Centres of Excellence

(CoEs) in AI and AVGC-XR to drive innovation,

advanced research, skill development, and

global investments in emerging technology

sectors. These functions will be handed over to

the dedicated mission for emerging technologies,

once it is fully established.
